name: Aaron Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play basic electric bass for a neighbourhood theatre, record simple rhythm loops and help a qualified tutor teach beginning players. I drove deliveries until four years ago; I finished secondary school, and at 58 I am still the junior player who asks twice before changing a chord.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a paid week mean now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner has part-time care shifts, and our children are grown. We have about three weeks of expenses saved and I earn less than most musicians, so I cannot count an unconfirmed pension as our next paycheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that a quicker booking sheet is fine if the bass player still gets a paid call. I would keep asking the tutor what the beginners need from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three weeks of savings and few nearby junior music posts make an ordinary cancelled show serious. My partner’s care shifts vary too, so a plateau does not make the household secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep the paid bass calls, rhythm loops and two supervised beginner sessions. I use AI now and then to organise practice notes, but I play each pattern myself before giving it to a learner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the ordinary gaps. I cannot spend a promised show fee at the food shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has a promised show failed to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The autumn fair closed early and the theatre paid only half the call. I would ask for the cancellation amount in writing before the next outdoor date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your grown children for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes to manage. I might ask for a lift, but I would not put their wages in our budget.

I would ask the tutor what **beginners need** from me.
think: Our **three-week reserve** makes a cancelled show serious.
Variable **care shifts** and few nearby jobs limit the household cushion.
do: Keep **paid bass calls**, rhythm loops and supervised beginners this month.
Request a **written cancellation amount** before the next outdoor date.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current gaps in our wages.
S0.quote: I cannot spend a promised show fee at the food shop.
fieldNote: His **late junior start** follows delivery work; neither his skill nor savings supports an easy exit.
His **occasional AI notes** are checked by playing before learners receive them.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre bass calls, rhythm loops and supervised beginners
Request written cancellation amount before next outdoor date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre committee that software may make the simple rhythm loops I sell. I would ask for paid live calls and a written fee for helping the tutor, and I would support the players’ association asking the same for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loops are around a quarter of my small pay. If those sales fall, I cannot fill the gap by claiming I am ready to lead a class alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would take loop invoices to the players’ association and request written paid assistant hours. In the first year I would attend the senior tutor’s paid lesson on a new rhythm checker, then test only a loop I own with no pupil names if the centre approves local storage; I would play each suggested beat and stop if it changes the rhythm or leaves the centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing recording fees. I am willing to learn a proven tool, but the class still needs a paid adult.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you use a child’s practice recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A child’s voice and name stay in the lesson folder; I would test a nameless loop I made myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply for other work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If paid loops or assistant hours actually fall, I would apply for a posted paid theatre music assistant role only if my secondary education and experience qualify, its written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the hours fit my partner’s care rota; I would keep current calls until a signed offer. I would ask for the written hours before I apply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the theatre that AGI by 2028 may make the loops and score notes without me. I would ask for signed paid calls for the people still setting up and playing live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the loop sales to stop in 2028 and fear the theatre may shorten paid bass calls. Robots that carry and play instruments come around 2031, three years later; the loop income goes before the cases move themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would total the loop invoices and request a signed paid theatre calendar. In the first year after 2028, if bass calls also fall, I would apply for a posted community-centre music assistant job only if my schooling and supervised teaching experience qualify, its written net pay after travel replaces lost calls and transport fits our care-shift car schedule; I would keep paid theatre and tutor work until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about likely loop losses; I would be alarmed if bass calls also fell, taking most of my pay. I have lain awake wondering whether three weeks of savings would cover our next rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a certificate before applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if an actual posted job requires it and the course has funded tuition or paid study hours. I cannot spend the last of our reserve on an unfunded music course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Will you stop working at 60 if that happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 in 2028, but I have not checked a pension amount and cannot assume it pays the rent. I would request a written estimate while keeping paid work.

I would ask for **signed paid calls** for live players and setup workers.

do: Count **loop invoices** and request a signed theatre calendar now.
Apply for **posted music assistance** after 2028 bass cuts if qualified; written net after travel replaces losses, transport fits.
Keep **paid work** until written offer; request actual pension estimate; take posted-role-required certificate only with funded tuition or paid study time.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely recording losses; additional class or live-call cuts would alarm me.
S2.quote: I cannot spend the last of our reserve on an unfunded music course.
fieldNote: His **2028 loop loss** arrives before instrument-playing robots around 2031.
The **centre move** needs actual bass cuts, qualified posting, written net replacement, transport and signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the tutor that five years until AGI by 2031 is time to earn a proper assistant certificate. I would rather have a paid classroom than sell another cheap loop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loop sales may go by 2031, and robots that play bass arrive around 2034. A qualified class assistant could work longer, but a course with no wage attached is a poor bet for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would take a six-month community-music assistant course only if an actual centre offers a funded place, paid training hours and a timetable that fits my partner’s care shifts without losing her pay. In the first year after 2031, if paid loop or bass hours fall, I would apply for a posted paid class-assistant role only if the certificate qualifies me, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and transport works; I would keep theatre calls and supervised pupils until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the certificate leads to real paid hours. I cannot call an unpaid course preparation for retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a class alone after the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The senior tutor must observe my first sessions and sign off before I handle six beginners without help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is free but hours are unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid theatre shifts and wait for a paid intake. Free tuition would still cost us wages.

I would prefer a **paid classroom** to another cheap loop.
think: **Loop income** may go by 2031 before 2034 playing robots.
A **paid assistant post** matters more than an unfunded certificate.
do: Take a **funded assistant course** only with offered place, paid hours and care rota without lost partner pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the players’ association that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to get paid training and honest retirement figures. I will be 68 then. An age on a calendar is not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loops could stop paying by 2036, and robots may take live instrument calls around 2039. With three weeks of savings today, waiting for a distant date would be foolish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I would request a written pension estimate and save five percent of each extra paid beginner lesson after rent, food and travel, aiming for two months. In the first year after 2036, if music fees fall, I would keep paid calls and apply for a posted centre class-assistant role only if my schooling and supervised experience qualify, written net pay after travel covers lost music fees and transport works; I would leave only after a signed offer states hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay anxious because the next dry month matters more than the far-off headline. A written pension estimate will tell me what I may receive, not replace this year’s wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension estimate is small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep working and ask the association about paid jobs I can still do. I will not mark myself retired on the basis of a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no extra lesson fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I save nothing new that week. I cannot put the same grocery money in two envelopes.

fieldNote: The **pension estimate** is a fact-finding step, not assumed retirement income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both loop sales and bass calls could fall before I know what retirement income is real. Signed theatre dates, a posted qualified assistant job and a written pension estimate would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who will sit beside the first nervous learner. A paid class needs a teacher who notices the player, not just the pattern.

headlineQuote: A paid class needs a teacher who notices the player, not just the pattern.
portrait: At **58**, Aaron is a junior bassist who left deliveries four years ago and completed secondary school.
His **lower pay**, three-week reserve and few nearby music jobs make cancelled calls a serious household risk.
He uses **AI occasionally** and tests a new checker only with paid instruction, approved storage and manual playing.
A **funded assistant course** needs paid hours and no lost partner pay before a qualified posted job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove loop sales and paid bass calls before he builds a reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed theatre dates**, a qualified posted assistant role and a written retirement estimate would help Aaron.
